newsitem.title: JAPAN: Yen fall makes Japan firms mull shift back home.
newsitem.headline: Yen fall makes Japan firms mull shift back home.

text.p: A sharp slide in the yen is encouraging Japanese firms to rethink their drive to shift manufacturing overseas, and is making some consider bringing part of that production back home.
Economists say the trend could pick up if the yen sticks at its current low levels or falls further, but add that a wholesale pullout from overseas production is not on the cards.

"Japan will be taking jobs from other parts of the world because of the weakening of the yen. It's happening already and if the yen stays at this level, it will happen to a further extent," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.

Japanese firms have been shifting output offshore since the mid-1980s when the yen began a relentless climb against the dollar. The trend got another strong nudge when the Japanese currency started to soar again in spring of 1993, rising to a global record high of 79.75 to the dollar in April 1995.
The moves raised the spectre of a "hollowing out" of Japan's economy, accompanied by high structural unemployment.
A stronger currency makes a country's exports less price-competitive abroad, while a weaker one boosts their allure to overseas customers.

Pressed by the strong yen, big Japanese manufacturers have cut costs so exports can be profitable when the yen is around 105 to the dollar or lower, while the break-even point for smaller firms is now about 108 yen, economists say.

Now, however, expectations that Japanese interest rates will stay at rock-bottom levels have sharply weakened the yen, which fell to within a hair's breadth of 115 to the dollar on Tuesday. The yen has since recovered a bit, but the outlook remains bearish.

Honda Motor Co Ltd said last week it might move production of its popular estate model, the Accord Wagon, back to Japan from the United States, adding that the possible shift was part of its policy of making products where they sell best.

Industry sources said on Wednesday that Toyota Motor Corp would produce its Scepter Wagon, to be launched here next year, domestically, but added that a shrunken U.S. station wagon market, not the yen's weakness, was behind the move.

And Sony Computer Entertainment Inc, a unit of Sony Corp also said it was boosting output of its Playstation game players in Japan, while halting production in the United States, to reap the benefits of larger-scale production.

Given the huge cost of existing overseas investments and the persistent lure of foreign markets, especially in the rest of Asia, Japanese firms are unlikely to repatriate huge chunks of overseas production.

"It will certainly happen at the margins," said Ron Bevacqua, an economist at Merrill Lynch Japan. "But the whole shift of production abroad is a process that is continuing. I don't think we will see a reversal of the shift to Asia.
"There were two impetuses for the moves. One was high domestic costs. But the more important reason is growing markets abroad, and these markets are still going to grow."
Nor are firms necessarily convinced that the yen will stay weak forever. "They have the number 79.75 indelibly imprinted in their minds," Bevacqua said. "They won't forget that."

Pressure to procure components overseas to get cheaper prices, however, has eased, and companies mulling where to make new products and models may well decide to do so in Japan rather than overseas, economists said.
"The old assumption that Japan would be just an R&D (research and development) hub and produce overseas was a popular story," said Chris Calderwood, chief economist at BZW Securities.
"The weaker yen will stop production that is here from being sent abroad and encourage companies to roll out their newest models and products in Japan," he said.
